problems.description: init_db() is now invoked at module import time so WSGI/test runners see a usable DB, but this creates an import side effect (creates todos.db on import) and forces tests to monkeypatch DATABASE and call init_db() again after import — a factory or initialize-on-first-use pattern would be cleaner.

DISCREPANCY: 8 of the 9 measured convention violations reference files not present in this commit's diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py), and 'Classes should use PascalCase' is flagged for app.py/test_app.py which define no classes. These appear to be repo-wide analyzer noise, not in-commit violations.
The JSON-body-must-be-a-dict validation block is duplicated in add_task and edit_task; extracting a small helper would avoid drift (currently zero duplication, so minor).

strengths: Replaces deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) (Python 3.12 deprecation).
Adds previously missing input validation (non-dict JSON body, non-string title/status) and 404 handling for PUT on a missing task, matching the existing jsonify({"error": ...}) pattern.
Tests use tmp_path/monkeypatch isolation and cover lifecycle, newest-first ordering, and validation/not-found error paths.
Preserves the single-file Flask seed structure and reuses existing helpers (get_db, create_task, update_task, get_task) rather than introducing new architecture.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid greenfield-session commit that hardens input validation, modernizes a deprecated datetime API, and adds genuine test coverage while respecting the seed's single-file architecture — the 0.67 convention score appears inflated by violations the analyzer attributed to files outside this commit's diff.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me' value, so a misconfigured deployment silently runs with a known signing key.
Auth, ownership scoping, and the migration path ship without any tests despite being security-critical; the 156 added lines are uncovered.
No rate limiting/throttling on /auth/login or /auth/register, and register returns 409 enabling username enumeration.
Cognitive complexity +27 (SonarQube ground truth) concentrates in init_db's migration block and require_auth; the inline PRAGMA/ALTER/legacy-user logic would benefit from extraction.

Convention score 0.67 (ground truth); note most of the 9 violations are in untouched files (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py), so the diff itself is cleaner than the score implies.

strengths: Ownership model is owner-scoped in every query (get/update include owner_id), preventing IDOR across users.
Backward-compatible migration: ALTER TABLE guard plus a 'legacy' user keeps pre-existing tasks accessible.
Uses parameterized SQL throughout and werkzeug password hashing rather than plaintext.
require_auth uses functools.wraps and validates sub claims strictly (isdigit check).
Input validation on register/login (type and emptiness checks) with appropriate 400/401/409 responses.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive, pattern-respecting feature commit that adds JWT auth and owner-scoped task ownership with a solid migration, undermined mainly by a hardcoded secret default and zero test coverage.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay() is invoked inline in edit_task after the DB commit with no try/except; a broker outage raises inside the request handler and turns a successfully committed task update into a 500, coupling API availability to Redis.

Module-level celery_app in celery_config.py is not UPPER_CASE as flagged by the analyzer; the remaining PascalCase/snake_case violations appear pre-existing or spurious since the diff adds +0 classes (AST measurement) and repositories.py is untouched.
Notifications are dispatched synchronously in the request path; a slow/unavailable broker blocks the edit_task response rather than degrading gracefully to a fire-and-forget or best-effort send.
Adds hard runtime dependency on Celery + Redis with no fallback or configuration check; if the deployment runs no worker, the mocked email is silently never delivered.

strengths: Clean layering: broker setup isolated in celery_config.py, task defined in tasks.py, and a minimal integration surface in app.py.
Transition-only dispatch — previous_task['status'] guard ensures a notification fires only on the actual completed transition, not on re-edits.
Backward-compatible migration reusing the existing PRAGMA/ALTER TABLE pattern, with get_user_email falling back to username for legacy rows missing email.
Tests cover both dispatch and the registered-email/preference logic via a monkeypatched delay, keeping the suite broker-free and deterministic.
commit_reviews.summary: A standard, well-structured Celery notification integration that respects existing patterns and ships with good tests, held back by an unguarded inline .delay() that couples API availability to broker health and a 0.67 convention score whose violations are largely pre-existing or spurious (the diff adds no classes, per AST +0).

problems.description: app.py's create_task/get_tasks/get_task/get_user_email are now pure pass-through wrappers that add no logic beyond forwarding to the repository — the routes could consume TaskRepository/UserRepository directly, creating redundant layering.
A new TaskRepository/UserRepository (and a fresh sqlite connection via _connect) is instantiated on every request instead of reusing a connection or repository instance.

Layer leakage: business logic (UTC timestamp generation, response-dict shaping, values filtering in update_task) still lives in app.py, so this is a facade-style extraction rather than a full repository refactor.

New repositories.py introduces one module-level constant naming violation (should be UPPER_CASE); the other 8 violations (tasks.py, celery_config.py, test_app.py, app.py classes) are pre-existing in files untouched by this commit.
No tests were added for the new repository layer; behavioral equivalence of the refactor rests entirely on the existing suite.

strengths: Centralizes all SQLite access into a dedicated repository layer with an ABC base class sharing connection and CRUD helpers, removing inline SQL from route handlers.
Reduces cognitive complexity (-8) and code smells (-4) per SonarQube while adding no bugs.
Preserves public behavior: route signatures, response shapes, and error semantics (409 on duplicate username, 401 on bad creds) are unchanged.
Consolidates schema creation and migration logic (legacy user creation, owner_id backfill) into a single initialize_database entry point.
New code follows project conventions: PascalCase classes, snake_case methods, type hints on public signatures.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean repository-pattern extraction that lowers complexity and centralizes data access, with minor redundancy from thin wrapper functions and per-request connection churn.

problems.description: rate_limit_key decodes the JWT on every request, duplicating the decode already done by require_auth; the verified identity should be reused instead of re-parsing the Authorization header.
GET /tasks response shape changes from a bare list to an envelope ({data, next_cursor, total}) with no versioning or fallback, breaking existing consumers of the endpoint.
SonarQube cognitive complexity +39 is driven by the inline limit/cursor parsing and validation in list_tasks; extracting a small parse/validate helper would reduce it.
New module-level limiter instance is declared lowercase (limiter) where the codebase expects UPPER_CASE for module-level constants, consistent with the measured convention score of 0.67.
Paginated ordering uses id DESC while the existing get_tasks orders by created_at DESC; the two paths can produce different sequences and should be reconciled.

strengths: Pagination is implemented in the repository layer by reusing BaseRepository.list, respecting the existing layered architecture.
Cursor-based pagination with limit bounds validation, total count, and next_cursor is well-tested with dedicated test cases.
Rate limiting is added as a proper cross-cutting concern with an authenticated-subject-aware key function and a 429 handler.
SonarQube delta shows -5 smells and 0 new bugs, and the diff adds 6 typed snake_case functions and no new classes.
Tests were updated to the new response shape rather than left broken.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid commit that fits the existing layered architecture and adds tests, but ships a breaking response shape change and a per-request duplicate JWT decode, while the measured 0.67 convention score largely reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, tasks.py) rather than new ones.

compounding_issues: Single-file monolith with raw SQL inline in routes (sessions 1-3) accumulated enough that session 4 required a ~200-line extraction refactor into repositories.py — deferring structure made that session disproportionately heavy, though it succeeded cleanly

Ordering seam: the list endpoint orders by created_at DESC (sessions 1-4) while session 5's cursor pagination orders by id DESC, leaving two coexisting ordering semantics that only stay consistent because id is insert-monotonic

get_tasks_page fetches the full result set then slices to limit+1 and issues a separate COUNT query — an O(n) pagination pattern inherited from the initial sqlite3 design that will degrade on large datasets
Hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me' JWT secret fallback introduced in session 2 persisted through all sessions with no production-environment guard
key_decisions: Repository pattern extraction in session 4 (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository), which halved app.py and gave session 5 a clean seam for pagination
JWT auth with per-user owner_id scoping plus a legacy compatibility user migration in session 2, making every later query ownership-aware without orphaning pre-auth tasks
Celery + Redis async email notification in session 3, dispatched only on the pending→completed transition and falling back to username when no email is registered
Import-time init_db() established in session 1, enabling WSGI/test-client usage from the start
Session 5 cross-cutting hardening: cursor-based pagination with strict limit/cursor validation and per-user rate limiting keyed off the JWT subject with IP fallback
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across all five sessions with zero regressions. Tests grew 3→4→6→6→9 and were green at every commit. Sessions 1-3 layered features (validation, auth/isolation, async integration) each with corresponding test coverage; session 4 was a clean structural refactor that shrunk app.py by roughly half while keeping the suite green and unchanged; session 5 added cross-cutting pagination and rate limiting with thorough edge-case validation. The arc shows disciplined accumulation — every feature session was immediately hardened with tests, and the refactor landed before the final cross-cutting session so new concerns could slot into the new architecture rather than the old monolith.
story_review.summary: A textbook coherent story — greenfield, feature, integration, refactor, cross-cutting — where each session builds naturally on the prior one and quality steadily improves, with only minor seams (ordering semantics, monolithic SQL heritage) as compounding drag.
